summary: Examines the problems of using MIME security multiparts and gateways to non-MIME mail systems. It points out how conversion can break signatures and other protection. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: If a sealed letter is rewritten by someone translating it, the seal no longer matches. This explains how translation between mail systems can break the seals.

questions: why do mail gateways break mime security
why do mail gateways break mime signatures
what is a security multiparts compliant gateway
should a gateway remove a signature when unpacking mime
subtitle: What mail gateways to non-MIME systems must do so signed and encrypted messages are not silently broken.

tldr.problem: Signed and encrypted MIME messages need to stay whole and end to end, but gateways to non-MIME systems often have to take messages apart and convert them. These needs cannot all be met at once.
tldr.mechanism: Since no single behavior works, the RFC requires gateways to offer several: tunnel security multiparts untouched, or take them apart with the signature kept and flagged, with per-user choice and optional signing or decrypting that is off by default.
tldr.outcome: A gateway that meets these requirements is called security multiparts compliant. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 2480 is a Proposed Standard from January 1999, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the document that defines what a security multiparts compliant gateway is.

sections.title: Why Gateways and Security Clash
sections.content:
RFC 2480 looks at what happens when MIME security multiparts from RFC 1847 pass through gateways into environments that do not support MIME. Security multiparts add integrity and confidentiality to protocols that carry MIME objects (RFC 2045, RFC 2046).

The document does not define a new protocol or message format. It defines a set of requirements for gateway behavior, so that security multiparts can get through gateways properly.
sections.eli5: A gateway is like a border crossing between two mail systems that speak different languages. This document says how the border guards should treat sealed letters.

sections.title: Three Needs That Pull Apart
sections.content:
The RFC names three things that matter in a mixed environment.

  • Secure whole objects. Security must cover a MIME object in its entirety. A signature that covers only the data and not the MIME labels lets someone alter the labels without detection. Leaving labels unencrypted exposes information that could help traffic analysis. Composite objects such as multipart/mixed and message/rfc822 must be secured as a unit too.
  • Convert to non-MIME formats. Gateways have to turn MIME labels into other forms, such as a file extension or an OID, and take composite objects apart into a sequential list of parts. Otherwise the objects are unusable where MIME is not supported.
  • End-to-end security. An integrity service applied somewhere other than an end point leaves a region where tampering is possible. A confidentiality service handled mid-path leaves a region where the object travels in the clear, and usually needs distributed private keys, which risks theft.
sections.eli5: You want the whole letter sealed, you want it translated for people who cannot read it, and you want only the sender and receiver to touch the seal. You cannot have all three at once.

sections.title: Why No Compromise Works
sections.content:
The RFC says these three needs are fundamentally in conflict: it is possible to satisfy two at once, but not all three.

It also says the conflict is worse than it first appears. Usually a compromise that optimizes some average of the requirements is possible. Here it is not, because many real-world situations exist where any one of the three absolutely must be satisfied.

The RFC admits that overlapping security services and secure key distribution could work around the problem, but notes that such designs are quite complex, and complexity in a security system is highly undesirable.
sections.eli5: Normally you could settle for a bit of each. Here, different people need different things completely, so a half-and-half answer would fail everyone.

sections.title: What Gateways Must Do
sections.content:
Because one solution cannot fit, gateways must provide several. The RFC lists five requirements.

  1. A gateway MUST be able to tunnel multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted objects as monolithic entities if there is any chance that MIME capabilities exist on the non-MIME side. No change to the content is permitted, even when it is itself a composite MIME object. Exceptions apply only when one side cannot possibly support MIME, for example a voice messaging system.
  2. A gateway MUST be able to take apart multipart/signed objects, exposing the content and ruining the signature. In that mode it SHOULD NOT remove the signature. It SHOULD keep it and add a note that it will probably be invalid for checking the contents but may still hold valuable information about the sender.
  3. A gateway SHOULD let the choice between these two options be made per user.
  4. A gateway MAY offer to check signatures and decrypt content. This MUST NOT be enabled by default, because the security exposure has to be assessed first.
  5. A gateway MAY offer to sign or encrypt material going from the non-MIME side to the MIME side. This too MUST NOT be enabled by default.
sections.eli5: The guard must be able to pass a sealed letter along unopened, or open it for people who cannot read sealed letters and write a note saying the seal is now probably broken. Doing anything fancier needs the guard to be told to do it.

sections.title: Being Security Multiparts Compliant
sections.content:
The RFC says a gateway that complies with the above requirements is considered to be security multiparts compliant. The capitalized words (MUST, SHOULD, MAY and their negations) are used as explained in RFC 1123, with MUST NOT and SHOULD NOT as logical extensions of that usage.

In practice that means the two modes, tunneling and taking apart, are mandatory, per-user selection is recommended, and the two active features (checking or decrypting, and signing or encrypting) are optional and off by default.
sections.eli5: A gateway earns a badge if it follows these rules. The badge shows it handles sealed letters carefully.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is one sentence: this entire document is about security. The risks it deals with are the ones described in the problem statement, namely tampering with unprotected labels, exposure of content, and the weakening effects of not working end to end.

The defaults it sets reflect that. Features that let a gateway check, decrypt, sign or encrypt on behalf of others must be switched on deliberately, after the exposure involved has been assessed.
sections.eli5: The whole document is about keeping letters safe, so the safest settings are the ones used unless someone chooses otherwise.

items.title: Secure whole objects
items.text: Sign and encrypt MIME objects with their labels, as a unit.

items.title: Convert for non-MIME
items.text: Turn labels and composite objects into the other side's forms.

items.title: End to end
items.text: Apply and remove security only at the connection end points.
